Chapter 6

Exemptions & Waivers

The current RVV framework for individual exemptions, seatbelt and child-restraint dispensations, repealed provisions, and priority vehicles.

  • Article 87 — General Exemptions
  • Article 88 — Seatbelts & Child Restraints
  • Articles 89–90 — Repealed
  • Article 91 — Priority Vehicles

Chapter VI of the RVV 1990 is titled Ontheffingen en vrijstellingen — exemptions and statutory dispensations. In the current text, its operative provisions are Article 87 (general RVV exemptions), Article 88 (seatbelt and child-restraint exemptions) and Article 91 (priority vehicles). Articles 89 and 90 have been repealed.

The key principle is precision. An exemption does not mean “the traffic rules no longer apply.” It only allows departure from the rule or sign covered by the legal provision or by the exemption decision, and any restrictions or conditions attached to that decision remain binding.

§ 1 — General Exemptions: Article 87

Article 87 is a limited legal gateway: the competent authority may grant an exemption only from the RVV provisions and traffic signs listed in that article.

What Is an Ontheffing? Individual exemption

An ontheffing is an official exemption granted by the legally competent authority for a particular situation. It can allow a person, vehicle or operation to depart from a specified RVV rule or traffic sign, but only within the scope of the decision.

Do not confuse this with a built-in exception in the traffic rules or with a supplementary plate that limits the scope of a traffic sign. Those can apply directly without an individual Article 87 decision.

Article 87 Does Not Cover Every RVV Rule Exact statutory list

Article 87 expressly identifies the rules from which the competent authority may grant an exemption. The current 2026 text includes specified provisions concerning place on the road, stopping and parking, motorways and autowegen, erven, certain other traffic rules, and Article 62 only for specified traffic signs and road markings.

For sign-based exemptions, the current list includes C1, C2, C4, C6–C21, C22e, D2, D4–D7, E1–E3 and F7, as well as the traffic signals and road markings referred to in Articles 73, 76, 77, 78 and 81.

Important for 2026: Article 87 now refers to C22e in the emission-zone system. Older summaries that still list the former C22a/C22c combination are outdated.
Who Is the Competent Authority? WVW Article 149

For ordinary road-related exemptions, the competent authority follows the road-management structure in the Roads Traffic Act (Wegenverkeerswet 1994):

  • National roads: the Minister responsible for the road.
  • Provincial roads: the Provincial Executive (gedeputeerde staten).
  • Water-board roads: the competent water-board authority.
  • Other roads: the municipal executive (burgemeester en wethouders), or a body acting under its lawful delegation.

Seatbelt and child-restraint exemptions are different: under Article 149(2) of the Roads Traffic Act, they are granted by the CBR.

The exemption is limited

It applies only to the rule, sign, route, vehicle, period or activity covered by the decision. It is not a general licence to ignore the RVV.

Conditions are legally binding

Under Article 150 of the Roads Traffic Act, an exemption may be subject to restrictions and conditions. Acting contrary to those conditions is prohibited.

Do not assume a paper-copy rule

The RVV does not create one universal rule saying every Article 87 exemption must always be carried as a paper document. Follow the requirements stated in the exemption and by the issuing authority.

Article 87 is not a catch-all

Oversize, overweight or technically exceptional vehicles can require other exemptions under vehicle legislation and separate RDW procedures. Do not automatically classify those as Article 87 exemptions.

Ontheffing, Vrijstelling and Built-In Exception

In Dutch legal terminology, an ontheffing is normally an individual dispensation granted by an authority. A vrijstelling is a general exemption created by law or regulation for a defined category. A built-in exception is simply part of the rule itself. For the theory exam, focus on the legal effect: determine exactly which rule is displaced, for whom, and under what conditions.

§ 2 — Seatbelts & Child Restraints: Article 88

Article 88 regulates exemptions based on medical necessity; other seatbelt and child-restraint exceptions are found in Articles 59–59b.

The General Seatbelt Rule Article 59

Drivers and passengers of passenger cars, commercial vehicles, enclosed three-wheeled motor vehicles and brommobiles must use the seatbelt available for their seat. A passenger under 18 who is shorter than 1.35 metres must normally use an approved child-restraint system.

The rule is therefore not simply “every person in every motor vehicle must always wear a belt.” The RVV defines the vehicle categories, restraint requirements and statutory exceptions precisely.

Medical Exemption Article 88 + CBR

When an exemption from the seatbelt or child-restraint obligation is requested because of medical necessity, Article 88 applies. A written statement from a doctor may be required.

The exemption is granted by the CBR under Article 149(2) of the Roads Traffic Act. Article 88 provides that the exemption has a stated validity period of no more than 20 years, and the application costs are borne by the applicant.

Do Not Treat Work Situations as Automatic Exemptions

The original version of this chapter listed reversing drivers, delivery drivers and road-maintenance workers as if they were automatically exempt from the seatbelt rule. That is too broad. Rijksoverheid states that someone who must frequently enter and leave a vehicle for work can apply for a seatbelt exemption through the CBR; this is not the same as a universal automatic exemption for every courier or maintenance driver.

Built-In Seatbelt Exceptions You Should Know

🚕
Certain taxi drivers

Article 59 contains a limited exception for drivers during qualifying fare-paying taxi transport. It does not mean every taxi driver is always exempt; contract transport and certain wheelchair-taxi situations are excluded from that exception.

🚌
Certain bus passengers

Passengers in buses in which standing passengers are permitted do not have to use a restraint while standing. The same applies in scheduled urban or regional bus services within built-up areas as provided by Article 59a.

♿
Wheelchair passengers

Article 59 contains special restraint rules for passengers who remain in a wheelchair. This is not a blanket “no belt” exception: an appropriate vehicle or wheelchair-restraint belt or another approved construction must be used.

🛏️
Approved lying positions

Passengers using a designated berth are outside the ordinary Article 59 seatbelt rule, but must use the safety device intended for that berth when one is available.

Child-Restraint Exceptions Articles 59, 59a & 59b

The normal rule is that passengers under 18 and shorter than 1.35 m use an approved child-restraint system. The RVV contains several narrowly defined exceptions, including:

  • Taxi without a child-restraint system: a child under 1.35 m is transported on a seat other than a front seat; the ordinary child-seat requirement is disapplied in the circumstances specified by Article 59.
  • Third child in the rear: if two child-restraint systems are already installed and a third cannot be fitted, a third child aged 3 or older and shorter than 1.35 m may use a seatbelt in a non-front seat.
  • Occasional short-distance transport: under the conditions of Article 59b, a child aged 3 or older and shorter than 1.35 m may travel in a non-front seat using a seatbelt. This exception does not apply where that child's parent is driving or is the owner or keeper of the car.
  • Medical necessity: an individual exemption from a child-restraint obligation can be granted through the Article 88 / CBR route.
Exam Distinction

A rule written directly into Articles 59–59b is a statutory exception; an exemption granted to a particular person by the CBR is an ontheffing. Do not treat these as the same legal mechanism.

§§ 3 & 4 — Articles 89 and 90 Have Been Repealed

The current RVV retains the paragraph numbers, but Articles 89 and 90 no longer contain operative rules.

Do Not Invent “Other Waivers” Here Current law

In the current RVV text, Article 89 is repealed and Article 90 is repealed. There is therefore no current §3 or §4 rule creating a general category of event waivers, supplementary-board waivers or road-section waivers.

Traffic measures for events, access restrictions and supplementary plates can of course exist under other legal provisions, but they should not be presented as if they were the present content of Articles 89 and 90.

§ 5 — Priority Vehicles: Article 91

A priority-vehicle driver may deviate from RVV rules only insofar as performing the urgent task requires it.

What Is a Priority Vehicle? Voorrangsvoertuig

Under the RVV definition, a priority vehicle is a motor vehicle using the optical and acoustic signals referred to in Article 29. For Dutch emergency vehicles, that means the prescribed blue flashing/rotating signal and the two-tone horn to indicate that the vehicle is carrying out an urgent task.

If only one of those signals is being used, the vehicle does not meet the RVV definition of a priority vehicle for the special right-of-way rule.

Article 91 — Scope of the Exemption

The legal rule is broader and more precise than a memorised checklist: the driver may deviate from the provisions of the RVV only to the extent required by the performance of the task.

SpeedAn RVV speed limit may be exceeded when the urgent task requires it, subject to operational branch rules.
Traffic lightsA red light may be passed when task performance requires it and the applicable emergency-driving rules are followed.
Signs & lane rulesRVV sign, direction and lane restrictions can be departed from when necessary for the task.
Hard shoulderUse can be permitted when required, subject to the applicable emergency-driving limits.
The Exemption Is Not Unlimited Safety still governs

Article 91 is an exemption from the RVV; it is not a licence for reckless driving. The general prohibition in Article 5 of the Roads Traffic Act against causing or potentially causing danger or obstruction on the road still applies.

The national rules on optical and acoustic signals also require the emergency-service branch guidelines to contain operational limits. Those include, among other things, a maximum of 20 km/h when passing a red traffic light, a general limit of 40 km/h above the locally applicable maximum speed on the carriageway (with a narrowly framed police exception), and specific limits for use of the hard shoulder.

What Other Road Users Must Do Article 50

Article 50 requires road users to let the driver of a priority vehicle go first. Create space promptly and safely, and avoid blocking the route.

Article 50 does not give ordinary road users the same Article 91 exemption. Do not assume that an approaching ambulance, police car or fire engine automatically authorises you to run a red light, enter a prohibited road or make another dangerous manoeuvre. Make room in the safest lawful way available.

Which Services Can Use the Signals? Article 29

Article 29 covers motor vehicles used by the police, fire service, emergency medical services, and other emergency services specifically designated by ministerial regulation, when they use the prescribed signals to show that they are carrying out an urgent task.

Do not treat every vehicle with a coloured beacon as a priority vehicle. The legal status depends on the Article 29 signals and the urgent-task conditions.

Green Light — The Original Text Was Wrong

A green beacon is not a doctor's “courtesy request” signal. Under the current Dutch rules, green signal lighting is used on a stationary emergency-service vehicle to identify the vehicle of the highest-ranking incident commander. A green light by itself does not make a vehicle a priority vehicle and creates no Article 50 right of way.

Chapter 6 — What to Take Away

Article 87: the competent authority can grant an exemption only from the RVV provisions and traffic signs specifically listed there. The issuing authority follows the road-management structure in the Roads Traffic Act, and restrictions or conditions attached to an exemption are binding.

Article 88: medical exemptions from seatbelt and child-restraint obligations are handled through the CBR. Do not confuse an individual CBR exemption with the built-in exceptions already written into Articles 59–59b.

Articles 89 and 90 are repealed. Article 91 allows priority-vehicle drivers to depart from RVV rules only insofar as their task requires it. A priority vehicle uses the prescribed blue signal and two-tone horn, and other road users must let it go first under Article 50.

A green beacon identifies the highest-ranking incident command vehicle when stationary; it is not a doctor's priority signal.

Dutch Driving Theory — checked against RVV 1990 Articles 50, 59–59b and Chapter VI (Articles 87–91), the Roads Traffic Act 1994, and the Regeling optische en geluidssignalen 2009 (2026) 6
